newsitem.title: USA: NASD expected to file charges against First Albany.
newsitem.headline: NASD expected to file charges against First Albany.

text.p: The NASD is expected to announce shortly an enforcement action against First Albany Corp for alleged violations of Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board book- and record-keeping rules, knowedgeable sources said.

The National Association of Securities Dealers is likely to charge that the firm kept inadequate records of at least one payment to an outside consultant connected to a New Jersey bond issuer, the sources said.
A First Albany spokesman had no comment.

Enacted in March 1996, MSRB rule G-38 requires muni dealers to disclose information on a quarterly basis to the public about their arrangements with the consultants they hire to help them win bond business.

But NASD's charges are expected to involve First Albany's activities before 1996, the sources said. Therefore, the NASD is likely to bring the charges in the context of older board rules that require dealers to maintain adequate books and records concerning market activity, the sources said.
The action would be one of the first major cases brought by NASD against a firm for a G-38 violation.

An NASD spokesman said the association had no comment. Christopher Taylor, executive director of MSRB, also said he had no comment on the matter or on market speculation that NASD has as many as eight such muni enforcement actions in the works.
But Taylor did offer a general comment about the enforcement actions that market players may see out of the NASD and Securities and Exchange Commission in the coming months.

"I would remind people as we go through the summer and the fall that any enforcement actions by the NASD and SEC are for events that took place prior to enactment of board rules designed to strengthen the integrity of market," Taylor said.

The board developed an action plan in 1993 that led to enactment of the board's first pay-to-play rule G-37 in 1994, to G-38 in 1996, to an overhaul of price transparency practices, and other key regulatory changes.
"Market practice has changed dramatically since the middle of 1993, and people should not forget that we are in a new era, despite all of the stories that may appear," Taylor said.
